posts.title: You might not need more leads first

copy.default:
Most appointment-led businesses do not have a lead problem first.

They have gaps after the lead arrives.

Someone enquires but never books.

Someone cancels and never rearranges.

A client finishes their appointment without a clear next step.

A regular quietly stops coming back.

Those are very different problems.

But the response is often the same:

“Get more leads.”

Sometimes that is exactly what the business needs.

But before paying to put more people into the front of the journey, I would check where the people already inside it are disappearing.

More demand is useful.

Keeping more of the demand you already earned can be useful first.

posts.title: I am getting more comfortable telling prospects not yet

copy.default:
One thing I am getting more comfortable with in 222Emails:

Not every interested business should become a client.

If the database is tiny, there may not be enough opportunity.

If they cannot handle additional appointments, creating more demand is not automatically useful.

If the contact permissions are unclear, we stop there.

If there is no sensible segment to test, forcing a campaign makes no sense.

That means sometimes the recommendation is:

Do something manually first.

Build the customer base further.

Fix another part of the journey.

Then come back.

It is slower than trying to close everybody.

But I would rather qualify someone out than build a system whose economics I do not believe in.

posts.title: Four places I check before recommending more leads

copy.default:
Before telling an appointment-led business it needs more leads, I would look in four places:

1. Enquiries that never booked

Interest existed. What happened next?

2. Cancellations and no-shows

Was there a sensible route back?

3. Clients who left without rebooking

Was the next step ever made clear?

4. Previously active clients who went quiet

Did anyone notice when their normal pattern changed?

None automatically means “send more emails”.

They are diagnostic points.

Find where the journey is leaking first.

Then decide whether the answer is follow-up, process, capacity, booking experience, acquisition, or something else entirely.

posts.title: Reactivation is not email the old database

copy.default:
Reactivation sounds simple until you ask:

Who exactly are we reactivating?

A regular client who is slightly overdue is not the same as someone who visited once three years ago.

A cancelled appointment is not the same as an enquiry that never booked.

Someone who has already returned should not still be inside the win-back journey.

And somebody who should no longer be contacted needs to be excluded completely.

So the copy is not where I start.

I start with:

Who belongs in the group?

Why would returning make sense?

What should happen next?

What makes the journey stop?

Eligibility first.

Message second.

posts.title: Why our reactivation pilot lasts 14 days

copy.default:
Fourteen days is not enough time to “transform” somebody's business.

That is not what I want it to do.

The point of our Reactivation Pilot is much narrower.

Take one eligible group of previous clients or enquiries.

Choose one clear reason to return.

Run one controlled campaign.

Watch what actually happens.

Replies.

Interest.

Bookings where evidenced.

Objections.

Silence.

Operational problems.

Then make the next decision using something more useful than theory.

A pilot should reduce uncertainty.

Not disguise a sales pitch as a guaranteed result.

posts.title: The metric I care about is whether the customer state changed

copy.default:
Open rate can tell me someone looked.

It cannot tell me whether the business moved.

For a client-return journey, I care much more about what happened afterwards.

Did the enquiry book?

Did the cancellation rearrange?

Did the overdue client return?

Did the dormant client reply with genuine intent?

Did the journey stop when it should?

Opens and clicks can still help diagnose the message.

But the commercial job usually sits further down the journey.

The measurement should follow the outcome the system was actually built to create.

posts.title: If the business stops whenever I am busy I have built myself a job

copy.default:
I am studying, selling, building 222Emails and trying to make the business move faster at the same time.

That creates an uncomfortable test.

What stops working when I get busy?

If every follow-up waits for me...

Every decision waits for me...

Every lead handoff waits for me...

Then I have not really built leverage yet.

I have just created more things that depend on my attention.

That is one reason I have become obsessed with clear ownership and systems.

Not to remove people.

Not to automate everything.

To make sure the next useful action does not disappear because one person had a busy day.

posts.title: Four revenue leaks we inspect first

copy.default:
Four places we look first when an appointment-led business says it wants more bookings:

1. Enquiries that never became bookings.
2. Cancellations or no-shows with no sensible recovery route.
3. Completed appointments with no defined return path.
4. Previously active clients who quietly became overdue.

The question is not simply:

“Should we email them?”

The question is:

What happened, who is genuinely eligible, and what should happen next?

That diagnosis comes before the campaign.

posts.title: What the 14-Day Reactivation Pilot actually tests

copy.default:
The 14-Day Reactivation Pilot is deliberately narrow.

One eligible group.

One objective.

One campaign.

A controlled starting audience.

No automatic charge afterwards.

The purpose is to find out whether dormant demand inside the business responds when the right people receive a relevant reason to return.

It is not a promise of a particular number of bookings.

It is a structured way to replace assumptions with evidence.

posts.title: Booking software is not automatically a return system

copy.default:
Booking software can tell you what is in the diary.

A Client Return System asks what should happen when the diary changes.

An enquiry does not book.

A client cancels.

A no-show occurs.

A completed appointment has no next booking.

A regular becomes overdue.

The booking platform may already contain much of the information.

The commercial layer is deciding what those events should trigger, who owns the next action and when the journey should stop.

posts.title: Clean the dormant list before reactivating it

copy.default:
Before reactivating a dormant client list, separate the customer states.

Recently overdue.

Previously regular.

One-time client.

Past enquiry.

Cancelled appointment.

Already returned.

No longer eligible for contact.

Those groups should not automatically receive the same message.

The campaign is the visible part.

Eligibility is what keeps it relevant.

posts.title: Every recovery journey needs a stop rule

copy.default:
Booked.

Replied.

Opted out.

Moved to a person.

No longer eligible.

Every follow-up journey needs clear stop conditions.

Without them, automation eventually becomes noise.

Good automation knows when to act.

A good Client Return System also knows when to leave the customer alone.

Retention School

Define customer states before automation.

Enquired.
Booked.
Completed.
Cancelled.
No-show.
Due back.
Overdue.
Returned.

Define the states first.

Then define what moves someone from one state to another.

Only then build messages and automation.

Clear customer states make systems easier to understand, test and fix.

posts.title: Cancellation and no-show are different states

copy.default:
Retention School

A cancellation may come with notice and an intention to rearrange.

A no-show may require a completely different operational response.

Treating both as “missed appointments” can blur the next action.

For each state, define:

eligibility,
timing,
owner,
message,
human handoff,
and stop condition.

Precision makes follow-up more relevant.

posts.title: The business defines when somebody is due back

copy.default:
Retention School

The marketer should not invent the return window.

Use the reality of the service.

Booking history.

Business rules.

Normal service cadence.

Customer expectations.

Professional or operational constraints.

Then let the system identify when somebody genuinely moves from “active” to “due back”.

posts.title: Audit one journey manually before automating it

copy.default:
Retention School

Pick one journey.

For example:

Enquired but did not book.

Then answer:

What starts it?
What information exists?
What happens first?
How long do we wait?
What happens after silence?
When does a person take over?
What ends it?

If those decisions are unclear on paper, automation will not make them clearer.

posts.title: Measure the state change not only the message

copy.default:
Retention School

Did the enquiry book?

Did the cancellation rearrange?

Did the overdue client return?

Did the dormant client respond?

Did the journey stop correctly?

Opens and clicks can help diagnose a message.

They are not usually the final commercial outcome.

Measure the job the journey was built to perform.
